Our story

A family with a vision

At Tick Creek Ranch, we’re dedicated to restoring the health and vitality of our ranch through regenerative ranching. We believe in sustainable practices that promote soil health, biodiversity, and long-term productivity. Our goal is to create a vibrant ecosystem where both wildlife and cattle thrive.

We’re the White family — a family of eight and first-generation ranchers in Alton, Missouri. We’re building our ranch from the ground up and sharing the progress, DIY builds and all, on our channels as we go.

A land in need of healing

On the ranch we prioritize sustainable ranching practices that promote soil health and biodiversity. Our regenerative approach ensures the long-term vitality of our land and livestock. We believe in working with nature to create a thriving ecosystem for both wildlife and cattle.

On the ranch

Cattle & Horses

South Poll Cattle

We’re a family passionate about sustainable ranching and caring for the land. Our story is one of dedication, tradition, and a love for cattle and wildlife. We believe that healthy soil and happy livestock go hand in hand with a vibrant ecosystem.

PHOTO — horse photo [NEEDED FROM RANCH]

Quarter Horses

We use Natural Horsemanship training methods as we start all of our young horses. We don’t breed our own horses at this time — our young horses come from the Colt 45 Ranch in Oregon. We emphasize ground manners and round pen work, then expose each horse to different types of riding and ranch work, developing the areas they’re most inclined toward.

We’d love to help you find your next work or companion horse.

The Log Hopper

An ATV/UTV log-handling trailer for low-impact land maintenance and logging. Its walking-beam suspension lets it roll over stumps and brush, so you can go deep in the woods and come back out with the log.

  • 5,000 lbMile Marker winch
  • 620 lbTrailer weight
  • 3 inTubing, laser cut & welded here

Also: swivel ball coupler, deflectors against stubs and limbs, and a center trolley hook for hanging the choker chain.

Issue #2 · Latest

The year fences went digital: the biggest advances in ranching and ag tech

Satellite collars, a $3.7M Missouri project, drones that check cows, and an honest look at soil carbon.

This week we’re looking back at the biggest advances in regenerative ranching and ranch technology over the past year. A lot of it comes down to one idea: moving cattle without moving fence.

1. Virtual fencing comes to Missouri, at scale

In April 2026, the University of Missouri’s Center for Regenerative Agriculture announced it is expanding virtual fencing to the herds of 200 producers in Missouri and Nebraska, covering about 150,000 acres. A $3.7 million grant from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation pays for it, including incentive payments to producers who adopt the collars. The center first tested the technology with five Missouri producers. Source: Show Me Mizzou

Why it matters: virtual fencing is moving from early adopters to university-backed programs that help pay for it — and this one is in our home state.

2. Collars that talk to satellites

The biggest problem with virtual fencing has always been signal: no coverage, no fence. In April 2026, Halter launched collars that connect directly to Starlink satellites, with no cell towers or on-ranch radio towers needed. The company’s own modeling says this expands its coverage of the U.S. beef cattle market 2.5 times. Source: Beef Magazine

Why it matters: remote, rugged ground like the Ozarks has been the hardest place to make collars work. Satellite connectivity starts to close that gap.

3. Proof that cattle respect a virtual line

A year-long Oklahoma State University trial found cattle stayed inside virtual boundaries 96% of the time and sheep 99%, based on GPS data. Animals learned the system, and the electrical cues they received dropped over the study. The researcher recommended giving animals three days to a week to adjust. Most misses came from individual animals, poor collar fit, and technical issues like weak cell coverage. Source: Beef Central

Why it matters: the question is no longer “does it work?” It’s “how do we set it up well?” Collar fit and coverage make or break it.

4. Drones that check on your cows for you

Researchers at Thompson Rivers University in British Columbia are pairing GPS collars with “drone-in-a-box” units that launch automatically to a cow’s location, using infrared to check animals at night or under tree cover. In one case they cited, replacing fire-damaged barbed wire was estimated at over $500,000, versus roughly $86,000 for a virtual fencing system. The cost of collars and subscriptions is still a hurdle. Source: Farm Progress

Why it matters: collars tell you where an animal is; drones let you see it. Together they could save hours of checking pastures.

5. An honest look at regenerative grazing and soil carbon

Not every headline this year was a win. A review led by Woodwell Climate Research Center found 70 papers on whether regenerative grazing stores more soil carbon, but only 10 made scientifically robust comparisons — and those averaged no change. The researchers say the evidence is thin, not that the practice fails. Source: Woodwell Climate

Why it matters: if regenerative ranching is going to be taken seriously, it needs better data. That’s a reason to measure what’s happening on our own ground.

Industry watch

  • New World screwworm reached Texas. On June 3, 2026, USDA confirmed a detection in a calf in Zavala County, Texas, and set up a 20 km infested zone with quarantines and sterile fly releases. USDA reopened the Douglas, Arizona port to cattle imports from Mexico on August 24, 2026. Source: USDA APHIS
  • Prices strong, pastures dry. USDA’s July outlook raised its 2026 fed steer price forecast to $251.10 per hundredweight. About 46% of U.S. cattle were in drought-affected areas, up from 16% a year earlier, slowing herd rebuilding. Source: RFD-TV

Issue #1

Welcome to the ranch — and our brand-new website

Howdy, and welcome! Whether you found us through a Log Hopper video, a calf photo, or a late-night scroll, we’re glad you’re here.

We’ve rebuilt our website. For a long time, tickcreekranch.com was a single page. Now it’s a real home base for everything we do:

  • Our story — who we are and why we’re working to heal this land through regenerative ranching
  • Cattle & horses — our South Poll cattle and quarter horses, and how we start our young horses
  • The Log Hopper — the ATV/UTV log-handling trailer we designed and build here on the ranch
  • Virtual fencing — how GPS collars let us move pastures without moving fence
  • Tick Creek Trading Co. — TCR ranch wear, plus the gear we use day to day
  • Watch & follow — the best place to start with our videos and find us on every platform

What this newsletter is. Every week we’ll post one short read on where our industry is going: industry insights, new technology, and the ideas changing how land and livestock are managed. We’ll share what we’re reading, what we’re testing, and what we think it means for ranchers like us — no fluff, and no one paying for the opinions.

Come find us. More than 1.75 million people follow along across our channels. If you’re not subscribed on YouTube yet, that’s where the full stories live. Subscribe on YouTube →
